text: What does the current Developer Policy actually say, word for word, about how long we may keep message content, and how does that wording differ from the 2020 version?
answer:
**Ruling:** The current Developer Policy itself no longer contains a retention-duration clause; that duty now lives in the Developer Terms of Service, and it applies to "API Data" generally, not to message content specifically. There is no numeric time limit in either era.

**Why:** The retention duty in force today, effective from 2024-07-08, comes from the Developer Terms of Service, not the Developer Policy document:

> "you will (1) promptly update the API Data upon request from us or the applicable user, and (2) promptly delete the API Data when: (a) retaining it is no longer necessary for your Application's stated (and approved through App Review, as applicable) functionality that is permitted under the Terms; (b) you stop operating your Application (whether on your own, due to an enforcement action by us, or otherwise); (c) we request you delete it; (d) the applicable user requests you delete it; or (e) required by applicable laws or regulations."

Source: [Discord Developer Terms of Service (current, effective July 8, 2024) (Developer Policy)](https://support-dev.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles/8562894815383-Discord-Developer-Terms-of-Service)

By contrast, the 2020 wording sat directly inside the Developer Policy, as one bullet under "Handle data with care," effective from 2020-07-01:

> "retain data any longer than necessary for the operation of your application;"

Source: [2020 Discord Developer Policy (last updated July 1, 2020) (Developer Policy)](https://support-dev.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles/25279999805975-2020-Discord-Developer-Policy)

The knowledge base's edition-comparison entry confirms the 2022 and 2024 Developer Policy editions carry no separate retention bullet at all; the duty was folded into the Terms starting with the 2022 edition and repeated verbatim in 2024 (rule `retention-no-longer-necessary-2022`, same text, effective 2022-10-01 to 2024-07-07).

**Watch out:** The wording did more than move house. The 2020 standard was "necessary for the operation of your application," a broad, undefined bar. The current standard is "necessary for your Application's stated (and approved through App Review, as applicable) functionality," which ties retention to whatever you disclosed and, for privileged intents, whatever Discord approved, and adds four hard delete triggers (shutdown, Discord's request, the user's request, legal requirement) that the 2020 text never spelled out. Neither version names "message content" or gives a day/month/year figure, so any retention window you pick is a defensibility argument, not a citation.

**Counsel notes:** If asked in review why you keep message content for X days, point to your stated functionality, not to a clause that does not exist.

text: What does the 'Changes to Privileged Intent Access for Discord Apps' announcement say happens to apps that were already approved before June 10, 2026?
answer:
**Ruling:** Apps already approved for privileged intents before June 10, 2026 keep their access for now, but that access is no longer permanent: they must reapply annually, with a 90 day window to resubmit each time they are notified.

**Why:** Per rule `rule.intent-annual-reapply`, effective from 2026-06-10:

> If your app already has Privileged Intent access granted from a prior review, you're good for now, but you will need to reapply annually.

Source: [Getting Started with Privileged Intent Review (developer docs)](https://docs.discord.com/developers/gateway/getting-started-with-privileged-intent-review)

The support announcement adds the mechanics of that annual cycle: advance notice is sent by email and/or system DM before the reapplication date, then a 90 day window to resubmit, and missing that window removes access (though you can reapply any time). One line from the knowledge base entry on this page: "When your reapplication date approaches, you will receive advance notice via email and/or system DM, followed by 90 days to resubmit."

Source: [Changes to Privileged Intent Access for Discord Apps (developer support)](https://support-dev.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles/40281523410967-Changes-to-Privileged-Intent-Access-for-Discord-Apps)

**Watch out:** This announcement page itself prints no date (it says "Today, we're announcing…"). We date the change to June 10, 2026 based on the change log and the developer docs review guide, both of which carry that explicit date; the announcement's own metadata shows it was created May 6, 2026 and last edited June 11, 2026, so it should not be cited alone for the effective date.

**Counsel notes:** Previously-approved does not mean permanently approved anymore; put the annual reapproval date on a calendar, because Discord will not chase you twice.

answer:
**Ruling:** Payouts run on a monthly cycle, paid within 45 days after month end, with a $100 net minimum to trigger the first payout and a $25 net minimum for every cycle after that.

**Why:** The developer support article is the more specific source here and its rule is not superseded.

Effective from 2025-09-19:
> Eligible payouts will be provided within 45 days after the end of each calendar month. For example, for offerings purchased in January, you will receive payouts within 45 days after January 31st. An eligible payout can be defined as the first $100 earned [less applicable payment processing fees and transaction fees] and for the following billing cycles, in amounts greater than $25.

One more thing not in your question but worth flagging: there is also a 90-day window to dispute a payout after the payout date, per the Monetization Terms, separate from the 45-day payment cycle itself.

**Counsel notes:** Budget for the fees to bite before you hit $100, not after; "net" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

**Ruling:** Depends on your balance so far: you get paid once your app has earned its first $100 net of fees, then within 45 days after the end of each calendar month for amounts above $25.

text: How do I get into the App Directory?
answer:
**Ruling:** No, not yet. Before your app can appear in the App Directory you must complete Discord's App Verification (Stripe identity check for the team owner), then enable Discovery and meet the listing checklist.

**Why:** Discovery, which is what puts an app in the App Directory and App Launcher, is gated on verification.

Effective from 2026-09-19 (confidence: inferred):
> To enable **Discovery** for your app, we require your team owner to complete identity and application verification.

Source: [Enabling Discovery (developer docs)](https://docs.discord.com/developers/discovery/enabling-discovery)

The verification process itself, per the knowledge base, requires:
- The app must be owned by a Developer Team (not an individual account)
- The team owner must complete Stripe identity verification
- All other checklist criteria listed in the Developer Portal's App Verification tab must be met

Once verified, the App Directory eligibility rules (developer support, "App Directory Inclusion Guidelines," effective from 2025-10-09, confidence: inferred) add a content bar:
> **3. Do not host graphic or sexual content.** Graphic violence, sexual content, or other age-restricted topics are not allowed in public spaces. Apps opting into discoverability should be appropriate for audiences of all ages 13+.

Source: [App Directory Inclusion Guidelines (developer support)](https://support-dev.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles/8852009977879-App-Directory-Inclusion-Guidelines)

The App Directory listing knowledge base entry also lists required Discovery Settings fields you must complete before enabling Discovery: Support Server, Application Description, at least 1 tag (up to 5), and an Install URL, plus a public Privacy Policy and Terms of Service and compliance with the ToS, Community Guidelines and Developer Policy.

Once you enable Discovery, allow time for it to show up:
> Once you enable **Discovery**, it may take up to 24 hours for your app to appear in the App Directory and App Launcher.

Source: [Enabling Discovery (developer docs)](https://docs.discord.com/developers/discovery/enabling-discovery)

**Watch out:** Verification is not the same review as privileged intents (those are separate since the 2026-06-10 change), so being unverified does not by itself stop you from using intents or growing past any server count. There is an unresolved contradiction in the dataset (id C4) between an old support article claiming "verification is required for your app to scale past 100 servers" (dated 2024-08-30, superseded) and the newer separation-of-reviews rule. That does not change the App Directory answer above, but do not assume verification caps your growth, only your Discovery eligibility.

**Counsel notes:** Get the team owner's Stripe ID check done first; everything else in this checklist is paperwork you control.

**Ruling:** You can register up to 100 global slash (`CHAT_INPUT`) commands, 15 global user commands, 15 global message commands and 1 primary entry point command (same caps apply per guild for guild-scoped commands), and creating them is capped at 200 command creates per day per guild.

> * 15 global `USER` commands
> * 15 global `MESSAGE` commands

**Watch out:** Bulk `PUT` overwrites of commands that don't already exist also count toward the 200/day cap, so re-registering your whole command set on every deploy or reconnect can burn through it fast. Register once at startup and only push changes when the command definitions actually change.

answer:
**Ruling:** No, self-bots are banned outright, even for private or personal use, and doing this risks account termination.

**Why:** Community Guidelines rule 14, effective from 2025-09-29, is the highest-authority and current statement of this:

text: What data does my bot get from a server with zero privileged intents?
answer:
**Ruling:** With no privileged intents enabled, your bot still gets a fixed baseline of data from every server it is in, plus message content in a handful of exempt cases; everything else (member lists, presence, and message content in ordinary messages) comes back empty or is withheld.

**Why:** This baseline is separate from the intents system entirely.

Effective from page undated, snapshot 2026-09-19 (developer support article, no dated policy version cited):
> Basic user profile information of server members (usernames, avatars, banners, discriminators, nicknames); Roles that members have in the server; Metadata about messages (day and time sent); The voice channel members join, plus voice metadata (muted, deafened, streaming, video on); Message reactions by members; Language/locale selected by members in their User Settings

Source: [Bot Data Access & API Objects (developer support)](https://support-dev.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles)

On top of that baseline, without the Message Content intent specifically, content fields are empty except in defined exceptions:

Effective from 2026-06-10 (the newer guide; an older 2022 change log and the gateway docs page each list a narrower or slightly different set, all three are shown as conflicting in the ruling below):
> The Message Content intent is **not** needed for your app to access message content in these situations:
>
> * **Messages your app sends**
> * **Direct Messages sent to your app**
> * **Messages that @mention your app**
> * **Replies to your app's messages.** Note: this applies to replies sent using Discord's reply feature to a regular bot message (not an interaction response) and the user has "ping on reply" enabled. It does not apply to replies to slash command responses.

Source: [You Might Not Need a Privileged Intent (developer docs)](https://docs.discord.com/developers/gateway/you-might-not-need-a-privileged-intent)

**Watch out:** Three official pages give different lists of Message Content exceptions (the 2022 change log lists only three: own messages, DMs, mentions; the current Gateway docs page adds the target message of a message context menu command but omits replies; the June 2026 guide adds the reply/ping-on-reply exception but omits context menu targets). The dataset resolves this as a union of all of them rather than picking one page as authoritative, since each is incomplete rather than wrong. Without Guild Members or Guild Presences intents, you get no real-time member/presence events and no full member list, but you can still use Get Guild Member, Search Guild Members, Get User, and interaction-provided member data as approved alternatives.

**Counsel notes:** If your bot only needs data on demand from users who interact with it, you probably don't need any privileged intent at all, and enabling one "just in case" is itself flagged as a Developer Policy problem, not just an unnecessary risk.

text: My ## header shows as literal text in the message. Why?
answer:
**Ruling:** Your header is missing the required space after the hashes, so Discord renders it as plain text instead of a heading.

**Why:** Headers require `#`, `##` or `###` at the start of a line followed by a space, effective from 2025-04-23.

> **Note:** Don't forget to add a space between the leading heading character (`#`, `##`, `###`) and your text!
>
> To create a header you just need to include a specific number of the hash/pound sign character (`#`). Use (`#`) for a big header, (`##`) for a smaller header, or (`###`) for an even smaller header as the first character(s) in a new line to make a header.

Source: [Markdown Text 101 (Chat Formatting: Bold, Italic, Underline) (developer support)](https://support.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles/210298617-Markdown-Text-101-Chat-Formatting-Bold-Italic-Underline)

**Watch out:** the hashes must also be the very first characters on the line. If anything precedes them, even a space used for indentation, the line stays literal text too.

text: What is the maximum number of characters in an embed description, and in the whole embed?
answer:
**Ruling:** Description caps at 4096 characters, and the total across title, description, field names, field values, footer text and author name for the whole embed caps at 6000 characters.

**Why:** From the Message resource, effective from 2026-09-19 (page undated, snapshot 2026-09-19, confidence inferred):

> | title | 256 characters |
> | description | 4096 characters |
> | fields | Up to 25 field objects |
> | field.name | 256 characters |
> | field.value | 1024 characters |
> | footer.text | 2048 characters |
> | author.name | 256 characters |

Source: [Message resource (developer docs)](https://docs.discord.com/developers/resources/message)

And on the combined cap, same source and date:

> Additionally, the combined sum of characters in all `title`, `description`, `field.name`, `field.value`, `footer.text`, and `author.name` fields across all embeds attached to a message must not exceed 6000 characters. Violating any of these constraints will result in a `Bad Request` response.

Source: [Message resource (developer docs)](https://docs.discord.com/developers/resources/message)

**Watch out:** The 6000-character combined limit is per message across all embeds attached to it, not per single embed. A message can also hold up to 10 rich embeds, and that same 6000-character total applies across all of them together, so a description alone can use the full 4096 but leaves only 1904 for everything else on the message.

**Counsel notes:** Build embeds with a running character counter, not by eyeballing, since a Bad Request at send time is a bad way to find out you went over.

text: My bot sends a 3000 character message and gets a 400. A user says Nitro allows 4000, so why not for my bot?
answer:
**Ruling:** No, the 4000 character allowance is a Nitro perk for human users in the client, the bot API's `content` field is capped at 2000 characters regardless of anyone's Nitro status, so your 3000 character send gets rejected with a 400.

**Why:** The developer docs set the API limit, effective from 2026-09-19 (page undated, snapshot 2026-09-19, confidence inferred):

> Message contents (up to 2000 characters)

Source: [Message resource (developer docs)](https://docs.discord.com/developers/resources/message)

The Nitro figure your user is quoting is a separate, client-side rule for human accounts:

> You can raise the character cap limit to **4000** when you subscribe to Discord Nitro.

Source: [Sending Messages (user support)](https://support.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles/360034632292-Sending-Messages)

**Watch out:** Nitro changes what a human can type into the box in the client. It does not touch the `content` field limit your bot posts through via the API. There is no bot-side Nitro exception, verified or not, boosted server or not.

**Counsel notes:** Split the 3000 characters across two messages, or move the overflow into an embed description (up to 4096 characters) instead of fighting the content field.

text: How do I show a time that renders in each reader's own timezone, like 'in 2 hours'?
answer:
**Ruling:** Use the timestamp markdown tag `<t:UNIX_TIMESTAMP:R>`, where `UNIX_TIMESTAMP` is Unix time in seconds; Discord renders it in each reader's own timezone and locale, and the `R` style shows it as relative ("in 2 hours").

**Why:** Rule "Timestamps: <t:UNIX> or <t:UNIX:STYLE>, in seconds, shown in each viewer's timezone" (page undated, snapshot 2026-09-19, confidence inferred):

> Timestamps are expressed in **seconds** and display the given timestamp in the user's timezone and locale.

For the relative style specifically, the styles table (also page undated, snapshot 2026-09-19, confidence inferred):

> | R | 4 years ago | Relative Time |

Source: [API Reference (developer docs)](https://docs.discord.com/developers/reference)

Example: for a moment 2 hours from now, compute its Unix seconds value (say `1758312000`) and write `<t:1758312000:R>`.

**Watch out:** The number must be seconds, not milliseconds, and unix time not local time, or the rendered time will be wrong by orders of magnitude.

**Counsel notes:** Both rules here are marked inferred and the source page carries no explicit date, so I'm citing snapshot date rather than an effective date.

text: Does an unverified bot still stop at 100 servers?
answer:
**Ruling:** No confirmed cap exists any more, but Discord has not explicitly retracted the old "100 servers" rule either, so this is unresolved and worth confirming with Discord support before you rely on it.

**Why:** Two sources disagree (contradictionId C4).

Old rule, `effective from 2024-08-30`, still undated as "current" by its own page but pre-dates the June 2026 overhaul:
> Verification is required for your app to scale past 100 servers.

Source: [How Do I Get My App Verified? (developer support)](https://support-dev.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles/23926564536471-How-Do-I-Get-My-App-Verified)

Newer rule, `effective from 2026-06-10`:
> Previously, when an app hit 100 servers and was required to apply for continued access to its Privileged Intents, it was blocked from joining new servers until the review was complete. That's no longer the case. Under the new user-based threshold, apps can continue joining servers and reaching new users while their submission is under review.

Source: [Changes to Privileged Intent Access for Discord Apps (developer support)](https://support-dev.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles/40281523410967-Changes-to-Privileged-Intent-Access-for-Discord-Apps)

A companion rule from the same June 2026 change confirms verification and privileged-intent review are now separate processes entirely:
> Previously, App Verification and Privileged Intent review were part of the same review process. With this change, we have separated App Verification and the Privileged Intent review process.

Source: [Changes to Privileged Intent Access for Discord Apps (developer support)](https://support-dev.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles/40281523410967-Changes-to-Privileged-Intent-Access-for-Discord-Apps)

The dataset's own resolution note for this conflict: "Unresolved. The June 10, 2026 announcement says growth is no longer blocked during intent review and that verification is a separate process, and the Discovery docs describe verification only as the prerequisite for Discovery and monetisation. But no current page retracts the 100 server cap for unverified apps either; the only page that states it was last edited 2024-08-30. Our ruling: cite both, say no current source states a cap, and recommend asking developer support."

**Watch out:** You are at 99 servers today, one away from the old trigger point. The June 2026 change clearly removed the *intent-review* block on joining new servers, but it never says in plain words "unverified apps may exceed 100 servers." Nothing in the current docs frames verification as a growth gate any more, it frames it as the gate to Discovery and monetisation instead.

**Counsel notes:** Ask Discord developer support directly before you plan around crossing 100 servers unverified. Don't bet the roadmap on a support article's silence.
